claims.text: Coupled tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by passive-oxide-film dynamics.
Mechanical wear repeatedly disrupts the protective passive film.
The rate at which the passive film reforms in the corrosive environment controls overall degradation.
Slower passive-film reformation accelerates localized corrosion.
A stable, rapidly healing passive film limits coupled damage.
Standard annealing in air followed by controlled cooling can produce a uniform passive oxide layer on the high-entropy alloy.
The baseline alloy's composition and microstructure produce a naturally protective surface oxide.
A composition variant, surface pretreatment, or inhibitor can be used to destabilize the oxide or slow its reformation.
Removal of the protective oxide exposes fresh substrate that is more reactive than the passivated surface.
Rapid oxide reformation quickly repassivates exposed substrate and limits both corrosion and further mechanical attack.
When repassivation lags, localized corrosion synergistically enhances wear.
Slowing passive-film reformation will increase total degradation relative to a baseline having stable film dynamics.
Slowing passive-film reformation will increase wear loss relative to the baseline.
Slowing passive-film reformation will increase corrosion current density relative to the baseline.
The predicted mechanism applies under moderate mechanical loading and corrosive conditions in which oxide removal and reformation dominate.
The mechanism may cease to govern under extremely high mechanical stress that completely removes the oxide layer.
The mechanism may not operate in a non-corrosive environment.

contradictions.description: The prediction is conditional on the intervention actually slowing oxide reformation, but the falsification rule treats comparable reformation kinetics after pretreatment as falsification. Comparable kinetics would instead show that the manipulation failed and would not test the proposed causal relationship.
